Restructuring the Power Sector 
*355. SHRI RAMAMUNI REDDY SI RIGIREDDY: Will the Minister 
of POWER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the power sector is facing do or die situation; 
(b) if so, what steps the Ministry are taking or propose to take to 
restructure the power sector to make it commercially viable; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the SEBs losses amount to 1.8 per cent 
of the GDP of the country; and 
(d) if so, how the Ministry propose to recover the dues from the SEBs? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SURESH PRABHU): (a) to (d) 
Power sector is passing through a critical phase. The Gross Domestic 
Product (GDP) at current price during the year 2000-01 was Rs. 18,78,429 
crores. As against this cumulative commercial losses of SEBs upto March, 
2001 (without subsidies) were Rs. 26,013 crores (1.38 per cent of GDP). 
Government of India has recently approved a scheme for liquidating the 
present and future outstanding dues of the CPSUs against SEBs. Under the 
scheme 60% of the interest/surcharge on 
23 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2002] 
the delayed payments as on 30.09.2001 would be waived off and the rest of the 
dues would be securitised through tax-free bonds issued by the respective State 
Government.There would also be incentives to the States for timely payment 
of current dues. 
The Ministry of Power after wide ranging consultations with all stake holders 
namely state governments, State Electricity Boards, utilities, experts, trade 
unions, private investors and political leaders has evolved a compressive and 
detailed action plan for turning around the power sector. A broad strategy for 
this purpose was finalized in a Conference of Chief Ministers/Power Ministers 
taken by the Prime Minister on 3rd March, 2001. 
To tackle the problem of technical inefficiency at the level of distribution 
involving erratic power supply, frequent distribution transformer failures and low 
voltage with high technical losses, the Govt, of India has stepped into assist the 
States under the new Accelerated Power Development Programme (APDP). In 
the first phase of this programme 63 distribution circles in the States have been 
taken up for intensive upgradation. These identified circles are being developed as 
"Centres of Excellence" so as to serve as models for remaining distribution circles 
in the country for improvement in a phase manner. This programme has now 
become the Accelerated Power Development and Reform Programme (APDRP) 
and also provides for transitional financing. In this programme the Govt, of India 
had made an allocation of Rs. 3500 crores during 2002-03. The programme is being 
monitored by central level consultants who are required to undertake field level 
inspections. The intention is to replicate this programme in all the distribution 
circles of the country gradually. 
To support the reform efforts of all the States the Centre has been entering into 
MOUs with the states. These are State specific. In the MOUs, which have been 
signed by 21 States so far, the concerned States have committed to achieve 
milestones in reforming the power sector. The milestone include setting up of the 
State Electricity Regulatory Commission, timely payment of subsidies, metering 
of all 11 KV feeders, 100% metering of consumers, energy audit, reduction 
24 

[17 April, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
of technical and commercial losses etc.  Government of India has committed 
its support through additional allocation of power from Central Generating 
Stations, assistance for development of transmission system and financial 
assistance. 
A mechanism has been institutionalized for intense monitoring of the 
capacity addition programme both in the Central Sector as well as in the 
State Sector. The progress is being reviewed regularly. With the provision of 
adequate Plan funds and close monitoring, performance in capacity addition 
in the Tenth Plan is expected to show considerable improvement. Renovation 
and modernisation of existing plant is given priority. With the other 
measures for reducing technical losses in distribution and demand side 
management through energy efficiency and energy conservation, it should be 
possible to make the country free of power shortages. Basin-wise ranking 
studies have been undertaken by CEA so as to optimally utilize the total 
potential of feasible hydro projects over next few decades. 
Standing Committee on training has been eonsitutcd to formualte National 
Action Plan for Power Training. The Committee has submitted its report. A 
Committee has been constituted to draw up a perspective  research  and  
development  plan. 
The Conference of Chief Ministers held on 3rd March, 2001 resolved that 
Village Electrification may be completed by the end of the 10th Plan i.e. by 
year 2007 and full coverage of all households may be targeted for the end of 
the  11th Plan r.e.,  by year 2012. 
Rural electrification has not been included under Prime Minister's 
Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY) from the year 2001-02. 
In the Chief Ministers Conference, it wa s agreed that there is urgent need 
to dcpoliticisc power sector reforms and speed up their implementation. To 
explain the problems of the power sector  and the action that is required for 
resolving these problems, road show s have been organized across the 
country for generating public awareness and understanding. More than 2000 
road shows have been organized at the district level all across India. This has 
been considered necessary, as, without public understanding and support, it 
would be 
25 

RAJYA SABHA [17 April, 2002] 
difficult to implement to meausres necessary for turning around the financial 
and operational health of the power sector. 
The forward looking reform oriented electricity Bill 2001 has been 
introduced in Parliament. The Bill, inter-alia, contains stringent provisions 
for penalty in case of power thefts. The Bill also includes provision for 
reduction of cross subsidies, and for payment of subsidies up front by the 
State Governments to the State Power Utilities where such subsidies are 
considered unavoidable.

State Government. Retail tariff is determind by the State Electricity 
Regulatory Commissions (SERCs) or  by the State GovemmenfState 
Electricity Board where Regulatory Commissions have not been set up. 
Supply to agriculture sector in the country is by and large subsidized. Even 
in States where SERCs determine ta riff, the law empowers the State 
Government to give subsidies to a targeted group, if it so desires. The World

Resolutions of the Chief Ministers/Power Ministers Conference on

I. The Chief Ministers/Power Ministers took note of the challenges 
confronting the Power Sector. It was agreed that there is urgent need 
to dcpoliticise power sector reforms and speed up their 
implementation. For this purpose, an all-party consensus needs to be 
created. The Prime Minister is requested to convene all-party 
meetings including leaders of opposition in State Assemblies. 
II. The following Resolutions were adopted: 
A. COMPLETING   ELECTRIFICATION   OF   ALL   VILLAGES 
AND HOUSEHOLDS 
(i) Rural Electrification may be tr eated as a Basic Minimum Service 
under the Prime Minister's Gramodaya Yojana;

i.e. by year 2007; 
(iii) Full coverage of all households may be targeted for the end of the 
11th Plan i.e.  by year 2012. 
(iv) For the attainment of full electrification. States may be given flexibility 
for using funds under Rural Development Programmes with the 
consent of the Village/Block Panchayats for undertaking the task of 
electrification where it is required. 
(v) It was agreed that electrification of remote villages in the States 
would need a special mode of financing including an element of 
grant. 
B. DISTRIBUTION REFORMS 
The real problem of management and the challenge of reforms lies in the 
distribution sector. 
(i) Energy audit at all 11 KV feeders must be made effective within the 
next 6 months and accountability fixed at the local level. 
(ii) An effective Management Information System for this purpose. 
needs to be made operational. 
(iii) On the basis of the above, an effective program needs to be launched 
for identifying and eliminating power thefts in the next 2 years. 
(iv) Full metering of all consumers had been targeted for completion by 
December 2001. Special efforts sh ould be made to complete the 
programme. 
(v) The quality of power supplied esp ecially in rural areas needs to be 
improved through the APDP and other programmes quickly;

(vi) Commercial viability has to be achieved in distribution in 2-3 years 
through any or all of the following. 
—Creating Profit centres with full accountability. 
—Handing over of local distribution to Panchayats/Local 
Bodies/Franchisees/Users Associations, wherever necessary. 
—Privatisation of distribution. 
—Or any other means. 
(vii) Efforts by States, if necessary, at inviting private investment in the 
power sector need to be focusscd towards the distribution sector. 
(viii) Current operations on distribution would need to reach break even in 
two years and achieve positive returns thereafter. 
C. TARIFF DETERMINATION BY REGULATORY 
COMMISSIONS AND SUBSIDIES 
(i) State Electricity Regulatory Commissions may be made functional in 
the next six months and tariff filings made. Tariff orders issued by 
Central Electricity Regulatory Co mmission and State Electricity 
Regulatory Commissions need to be implemented fully unless 
stayed or set aside by Court order. It is necessary to move away from 
the regime of providing free power. 
(ii) Subsidies may be given only to the extent of State Government's 
capacity to pay the subsidies explicitly through budget provisions. 
(iii) The past decision of CMs of a minimum agricultural tariff of 50 
paise may be implemented immediately(*). 
D. GENERATION

plants through Renovation and Modernisation.

generation would flow only afte r reforms succeed in restoring

decisions regarding increase in outlays for the 10th Plan. Priority 
should be given for investments at those locations which produce 
the cheapest power specially for hydro projects and pit head thermal 
generation. CEA has estimated the requirement for an additional

An effective program in the field of demand side management through — 
energy efficient bulbs, tube lights and agricultural pumpsets, 
— time of the day metering and differential tariff for peak and off peak 
hours needs to be implemented with suitable mass awareness and 
extension efforts. 
F. SUPPORT FROM GOVERNMENT OF INDIA

Details of Project "Sustainable Community-Based Approaches to 
Livelihoods Enhancement" (SCALE) 
1. Objective, Duration and Area of Operation 
The SCALE project aims at undertaking field intervention to promote and 
demonstrate community-based natural resources management approaches around 
key resource issues for tangible and sustainable benefits at the local level, and at 
improving the policy framework as well as the implementation of policies impacting 
rural livelihoods through targeted research, advocacy, net working and training. 
The project components would be field implementations and an outreach 
programme. 
The field implementation component will be implemented in three districts in 
Gujarat and a fourth district in a semi-arid region in Gujarat or a neighbouring 
state to be selected during the Inception Phase. 
The wider outreach programme will be implemented in the semi-arid areas of 
India. 
The duration of the project will be 10 years. 
2. Implementation arrangements 
The Aga Khan Foundation (India) will have management res ponsibility for 
the project supported by relevant AKF offices elsewhere and other voluntary 
organisations. 
Components that fall under "Field Implementation" will predominantly be 
implemented through Aga Khan Rural Support Programme, India (AKRSP), is 
working in 450 villages in three districts of Gujarat, reaching out to over 
40,000 households.
